Build review · updated 25 August 2026

HanapGawa, honestly assessed

It is a real, working marketplace — not a mockup. Money moves through a correct escrow ledger and releases on its own when a client goes quiet, disputes are settled from photographs rather than from two people’s accounts of what happened, a provider cannot be booked into two places at once, and the privacy rights the app promises are buttons rather than an email address. Every screen below is a photograph of the running app. It is still not something you can point real customers at: nothing is wired to live SMS or live payments, there are no database backups, and no human outside this session has used it.

commit e7551f7 137/137 tests green ~15,000 lines 0 real users
8.4/10 toward launchable

The score is distance-to-launch, not quality of what exists. It has moved 6.5 → 7.1 → 8.0 → 8.4 across four build passes, each one closing gaps that did not need anyone else’s account. The latest pass added evidence photos, enforced availability, profile photos and an operations runbook — and, in the course of building them, found and fixed two real defects in the work of the hour before. What is left is almost entirely integration, operations, and the one thing code cannot supply — real users.

Marketplace flow
9/10
Post → offer → accept → start → done → confirm → review runs end to end, every step notifies the counterparty, a new post reaches up to 25 matching providers, the posting form tells a client what the job is worth, and a provider can no longer be booked into two places at the same hour.
Money & escrow
9/10
Integer centavos, append-only ledger, atomic state-claims, Serializable on Postgres. Escrow now releases on its own 72h after work is marked done unless someone disputes, so a busy client can no longer strand a provider's pay. Verified a ₱500 job auto-releasing exactly ₱440. No live payment processor attached yet.
Security posture
8/10
Hardened after an adversarial review that found a critical escrow-theft path, and a later self-review that caught a race in account closure. Rate limits now go fleet-wide with one environment variable. Still no independent penetration test — the one thing on this page I would not launch without.
Trust & safety
9/10
Contact masking genuinely works. ID documents are typed by magic bytes, stored off any web path, and deleted at decision time. An SOS button writes first and notifies after. Disputes are now settled from before/after photographs rather than from two accounts of the same afternoon. Still no PSA eVerify face match.
Mobile UX
9/10
Taglish throughout, thumb-sized targets, bottom tab bar, and now installable to a home screen with an offline card when the signal drops. Re-checked at 360px — the width of a budget Android. Still untested on real hardware.
Scale headroom
7/10
Clean modular monolith, indexed queries, Postgres-ready, and rate limiting that becomes fleet-wide by setting REDIS_URL. The “near me” sort still ranks within the newest 200 jobs rather than the whole set.
Production ops
7/10
CI runs typecheck, 137 tests, a seeded build, and smoke tests that assert protected routes reject anonymous callers and the escrow sweep fails closed without its secret. There is now a written runbook for whoever operates this — the daily loop, the 2am SOS call, how to decide a dispute. Still missing, and the highest-risk item on this page: database backups.

The honest ledger

What is genuinely finished, and what is not

Working and verified

  • ✓Full job lifecycle with a guarded state machine — money-moving steps can’t be raced or skipped
  • ✓Escrow hold, release, refund, and admin dispute resolution, all through one ledger
  • ✓Contact masking including spaced, dashed and spelled-out numbers, in English and Tagalog
  • ✓17 regions and ~130 cities with distance sorting
  • ✓Privacy boundary: no phone numbers, exact addresses or coordinates leak to non-parties
  • ✓Admin queues for KYC, disputes, payouts and abuse reports
  • ✓A critical escrow-theft exploit found, fixed, and re-tested as blocked
  • ✓Notifications on every counterparty-relevant event, scoped so you can only read and clear your own
  • ✓Password reset that revokes every existing session, with no account enumeration
  • ✓CI running typecheck, 100 tests, a seeded build, and smoke tests that catch an authorization regression or a mis-secured escrow sweep
  • ✓Escrow auto-release with a dispute freeze, so a client’s silence can no longer trap a provider’s pay
  • ✓ID documents typed by magic bytes, stored off any web-servable path, and deleted the moment a decision is recorded
  • ✓SOS and check-ins that record first and notify after — never rate-limited, never gated on verification
  • ✓Job broadcast to matching providers, so a new post is seen rather than sitting in an empty feed
  • ✓Price guidance from real completed jobs, labelled honestly when it is only an estimate
  • ✓Data export and account closure that anonymises in place, keeping the books and other people’s reviews intact
  • ✓Installable to a home screen, with a service worker that deliberately caches nothing personal
  • ✓Terms of Service and an RA 10173 privacy notice, linked from sign-up
  • ✓Evidence photos on a booking, visible to both parties and support, purged ninety days after settlement
  • ✓Availability that is enforced: a double-booking is refused, an out-of-hours booking only warns
  • ✓Profile photos served only to signed-in callers, with a support takedown
  • ✓An operations runbook: the daily loop, the 2am SOS call, dispute defaults, the 72-hour breach clock
  • ✓Error reporting that scrubs phone numbers, emails and sensitive keys before anything leaves the process

Missing before anyone pays

  • ×Live SMS — OTPs currently print to the server console
  • ×Live GCash/Maya money — the PayMongo path is written but has never processed a peso
  • ×Automated identity matching — PSA eVerify or a face match against the uploaded ID
  • ×Database backups. The highest-risk item here: losing the ledger loses the business, and unlike the rest of this column it costs almost nothing to fix
  • !A staging environment — every deploy currently goes straight to the thing holding people’s money
  • !Company name and Data Protection Officer details, still bracketed placeholders in the legal pages
  • !An independent penetration test before real money flows
  • !Any contact with a real Filipino user — the biggest unknown on this page
If you want this to earn

The next four moves, in order

Sequenced deliberately: each step is worthless until the one before it is done.

01

Show it to twenty real people before writing more code

Ten labanderas or cleaners, ten households, one city. Watch them use it on their own phones without help. Every assumption in this build — that they’ll accept escrow, tolerate masked chat, trust a badge — is currently untested. This costs nothing and can save months.

₱0 · 1 week
02

Wire the two integrations only you can open

A Semaphore SMS account and a PayMongo merchant account. The adapters are already written behind interfaces, so this is configuration and testing rather than new architecture. Until money actually moves, nothing else about the business is knowable.

₱6k–15k setup · 1–2 weeks
03

Register the business and lock the payment structure

SEC or DTI, BIR, mayor’s permit — and critically, the collecting-agent arrangement with your payment provider so you never hold customer funds yourself. docs/LEGAL.md lays this out. Do it before your first peso, not after.

₱20k–60k · 4–8 weeks
04

Launch one barangay-tight, category-narrow pilot

Two or three services in a single city — laundry, cleaning, errands. Density beats breadth: a user who finds someone within an hour comes back; a user who finds an empty feed never does. Add CI, monitoring and backups during this phase, while the blast radius is small.

the real work · 3–6 months
The one thing I would not skip

The adversarial review found a path where a client could accept finished work, open a dispute, and cancel to claw back the entire payment — the provider does the job and gets nothing. It is fixed and I verified the fix live. But it existed in code that looked correct and passed its tests, which is the honest argument for a real penetration test before you hold anyone’s money. On a platform whose entire promise is “hindi ka maloloko dito,” one such bug in production is not a bug report. It is the end of the brand.
